title: Tsuut’ina
body: A Dene-speaking First Nation located southwest of Calgary, Alberta. Tsuut’ina Elders explain the Nation’s name as meaning either “many people” or “beaver people.” Both interpretations are recognized by the Nation.

title: Tsúūt’ínà Gūnáhà
body: The traditional language of the Tsuut’ina Nation. It belongs to the Dene, or Athabaskan, language family and remains an important part of cultural identity, community knowledge, and language revitalization efforts.

title: Dene
body: A broad cultural and linguistic family of Indigenous peoples. The Tsuut’ina identify themselves as connected to the Dene through language, culture, customs, and historical territory.

title: Athabaskan
body: A major Indigenous language family that includes the Tsuut’ina language and the languages of many other Dene peoples across North America. Tsuut’ina is the only Dene-speaking Nation within Treaty 7 Territory.

title: Treaty 7
body: A treaty entered into in 1877 between representatives of the Crown and several First Nations of southern Alberta, including the Tsuut’ina Nation. Treaty 7 continues to hold political, historical, and cultural significance for the Nation today.

title: Chiila Bullhead
body: A historic Head Chief of the Tsuut’ina Nation associated with the Nation’s entry into Treaty No. 7 in 1877. His leadership is an important part of Tsuut’ina political and territorial history.

title: Treaty Territory
body: Land connected to the Nations that entered a treaty with the Crown. The Tsuut’ina Nation is one of the First Nations within Treaty 7 Territory in southern Alberta.

title: Sovereign Nation
body: A people with their own identity, political authority, community institutions, rights, responsibilities, and systems of governance. Tsuut’ina describes itself as a sovereign Nation and emphasizes its inherent and Treaty rights.

title: Indigenous Governance
body: The systems through which Indigenous Nations exercise leadership, decision-making, authority, and responsibility for their communities. Tsuut’ina identifies self-determination in Indigenous governance as an important part of Nationhood.

title: Self-Determination
body: The ability of a Nation to make decisions concerning its own people, institutions, culture, territory, and future. For Tsuut’ina, self-determination is closely connected with sovereignty and Indigenous governance.

title: Natural Law
body: A Tsuut’ina concept connected with the understanding that people, land, water, air, fire, and other parts of the natural world belong to an interconnected and sacred circle.

title: Sacred Circle
body: A way of understanding life as interconnected. Within the worldview described by Tsuut’ina Nation, human beings are only one part of a larger relationship that includes the land, elements, and other forms of life.

title: Oral History
body: Knowledge about the past preserved and shared through spoken stories, family accounts, teachings, and memories. Tsuut’ina recognizes that different families may carry different versions of historical stories.

title: Storytelling
body: A way of sharing history, knowledge, cultural values, and community memory from one generation to another. Storytelling is also incorporated into cultural experiences available through Grey Eagle.

title: Cultural Teachings
body: Knowledge shared about cultural values, traditions, relationships, history, and ways of understanding the world. Grey Eagle’s cultural experiences include opportunities to learn through Indigenous teachings and interpretation.

title: Cultural Protocols
body: Practices and expectations that guide respectful behaviour within cultural, community, or ceremonial contexts. Protocols may vary depending on the situation, family, or type of cultural activity.

title: Tsuut’ina Museum
body: A cultural institution connected to the preservation and interpretation of Tsuut’ina history, language, stories, and traditions. Grey Eagle Cultural Tours may include a guided cultural experience associated with the museum.

title: Cultural Tour
body: A guided experience designed to introduce visitors to Tsuut’ina culture, history, traditions, land, and contemporary Indigenous life. Grey Eagle offers several cultural experiences that can be customized for groups.

title: Buffalo Paddock
body: An outdoor cultural-tour experience where visitors can encounter buffalo while learning about their historical and cultural relationship with Indigenous peoples, land, and tradition.

title: Buffalo
body: An animal with major historical and cultural importance for Indigenous peoples of the Plains. At Grey Eagle, the buffalo becomes part of a guided experience connecting visitors with land, history, and cultural interpretation.

title: Indian Relay
body: A fast-paced Indigenous horse racing tradition based on horsemanship, teamwork, timing, and rapid rider transitions. Grey Eagle’s DH Ranch Indigenous Experience introduces visitors to Indian Relay and contemporary ranch life.

title: DH Ranch
body: A cultural experience featured through Grey Eagle Cultural Tours where visitors can learn about Indian Relay, horses, ranch life, and the teamwork involved in contemporary Indigenous horse culture.

title: Cultural Awareness
body: Learning intended to build a better understanding of another culture, including its history, values, traditions, perspectives, and contemporary experiences. Cultural awareness sessions form part of some Grey Eagle cultural offerings.

title: Indigenous Experience
body: An activity or program created to introduce visitors to aspects of Indigenous culture through direct learning, storytelling, interpretation, demonstrations, or interaction rather than information alone.

title: Living Culture
body: The idea that culture continues to develop through present-day language, families, artists, athletes, leaders, businesses, traditions, and community life rather than existing only as history.

title: Nationhood
body: The collective identity and continuing political, cultural, and social existence of a Nation. Tsuut’ina connects Nationhood with language, traditions, governance, economic development, and community life.

title: Tsuut’ina Day
body: A Tsuut’ina holiday observed on May 1. The Nation explains that the date is connected with the traditional beginning of another life cycle after winter and historically included community gathering, thanksgiving, decisions, feasts, and dances.

title: Treaty Day
body: A community occasion connected with Treaty No. 7. Contemporary Tsuut’ina Treaty Day celebrations may include activities that bring Nation Citizens and community members together.

title: Dàní’t’ádà
body: A Tsuut’ina greeting presented by the Nation with the meaning “Greetings” or “Welcome.” It is used prominently in official Tsuut’ina cultural communication.

title: Gújā Nágúdīgòy
body: A Tsuut’ina expression meaning “Good morning.” The phrase is included in the Nation’s official language-learning resources together with audio pronunciation materials.

title: Sīyísgáàs
body: A Tsuut’ina expression used to say “Thank you.” It appears in official Nation communications and is an accessible example of the language visitors may encounter while learning about Tsuut’ina culture.

title: Many People
body: One of the meanings Tsuut’ina Elders give for the name Tsuut’ina. The Nation recognizes both “many people” and “beaver people” as valid interpretations.

title: Beaver People
body: One of the traditional interpretations of the name Tsuut’ina recognized by the Nation’s Elders. Beaver imagery and related historical narratives also appear within Tsuut’ina cultural memory.

title: Beaver Bundle
body: A culturally significant bundle mentioned in the Nation’s publicly shared historical narrative about the migration and separation of the Tsuut’ina ancestors. It remains connected with cultural memory and continuity.

title: Tāstłāní
body: A dragon appearing in a publicly shared Tsuut’ina migration story. In the account, Tāstłāní breaks through the ice of a frozen lake, resulting in the separation of people who later continued in different directions.

title: Xani-tii Guk’a Sidodi
body: The Tsuut’ina name identified in the Nation’s migration story with Buffalo Lake, north of Edmonton. It is connected with the oral account describing the separation of the Tsuut’ina from other Dene people.

title: Indigenous-Inspired Cuisine
body: Contemporary food that incorporates Indigenous culinary influences, ingredients, ideas, or cultural inspiration. Dining can be added to some Grey Eagle cultural experiences, connecting food with the broader visitor experience.

title: Little Chief
body: A restaurant at Grey Eagle Resort & Casino whose culinary concept includes Indigenous influences. It can also form part of a broader cultural-tour experience when dining is included.

title: Cultural Interpretation
body: The process of helping visitors understand the meaning and context of history, places, traditions, stories, or cultural practices through guided explanation rather than simply presenting facts.

title: Cultural Heritage
body: The stories, language, knowledge, values, traditions, places, and practices carried across generations. In the context of Tsuut’ina Nation, heritage includes both historical knowledge and culture that continues in community life today.
